title: Rivas v. Overlake Hospital Medical Center
facts: Petitioner Susan Rivas filed a medical malpractice action against Overlake Hospital Medical Center three years and one day after complications from a renal angiogram and angioplasty performed at Overlake Hospital Medical Center caused her to lose a kidney. The trial court rejected Overlake Hospital Medical Center’s motion for summary judgment, ruling that although Rivas’s action was filed after the expiration of the three year statute of limitations, a genuine issue of material fact exists as to whether the statute of limitations was tolled pursuant to Washington Revised Code §4.16.190 during the four days Rivas was incapacitated while in intensive care following the loss of her kidney. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed and granted summary judgment for Overlake Hospital Medical Center, holding that the statute of limitations was not tolled insofar as Rivas’s incapacity did not meet the temporal and procedural requirements of the guardianship statute (Washington Revised Code §11.88). Rivas appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Must an incapacitated person meet the temporal and procedural requirements of the guardianship statute in order for §4.16.190 to toll the statute of limitations during their incapacity?
conclusions: Justice Chambers’ opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that §4.16.190 merely requires that a person be incompetent or disabled to such a degree that they cannot understand the nature of the cause of action when it accrues in order for the statute of limitations to toll and does not incorporate the requirements of the guardianship statute. Thus, as the Court held that a genuine issue of material exists as to whether Rivas was incapacitated to this degree while she was in intensive care, it remanded the case to the trial court.

title: In re Detention of Anderson; John Anderson v. State
facts: The respondent state of Washington petitioned the Superior Court for Pierce County to have petitioner John Anderson, a convicted sex offender whose release from a state psychiatric hospital was pending, committed pursuant to Washington Revised Code §71.09 as a sexually violent predator, asserting that his sexual relations with mentally disabled patients constituted, as required by the statute, recent overt acts creating a reasonable apprehension of sexually violent harm that justified commitment. The trial court subsequently ordered Anderson’s commitment. On appeal, however, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed the trial court’s decision and ordered a new trial, ruling that although Anderson’s conduct represented a recent overt act under §71.09, the trial court had erred in refusing to appoint Anderson’s requested expert to examine him and testify on his behalf. Anderson and the state of Washington cross-appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did Anderson’s sexual relations with mentally disabled patients incapable of consent create a reasonable apprehension of sexually violent harm? If so, should the trial court have granted Anderson’s motion to appoint an expert of his choosing to conduct a forensic psychosexual evaluation?
conclusions: Justice James M. Johnson’s opinion for the Court held that Anderson’s behavior fell within the terms of §71.09 insofar as it was sufficiently recent and akin, given the vulnerability of the sexual partners involved, to the sexual assaults on children that he had previously been convicted of. However, the Court also ruled that the trial court abused its discretion by refusing Anderson’s request to appoint his preferred expert to examine him and potentially offer testimony that would challenge the conclusion of the state’s expert that Anderson was likely to commit predatory acts of sexual violence if not confined. As granting Anderson’s request would not have unduly delayed the proceedings nor prejudiced the state nor imposed excessive costs on the state, the Court affirmed the decision of the Washington Court of Appeals to vacate the trial court’s commitment order.

title: In re disciplinary proceeding against Stansfield
facts: Petitioner Mark Stansfield was suspended from the practice of law for six months following a hearing before the respondent Washington State Bar Association’s disciplinary board, which found that Stansfield had violated Washington Rules of Professional Conduct §1.2(f) and Washington Rules of Professional Conduct §1.9 by purporting to represent a person without authority and by representing clients with adverse interests. Stansfield appealed the disciplinary board’s sanction to the Supreme Court of Washington, asserting that the disciplinary board had erred in failing to adopt the hearing officer’s findings regarding his motives and state of mind.
questions: Did the disciplinary board err in failing to adopt the hearing officer’s findings that Stansfield’s motives were beneficent and that his violations of rules of professional conduct were the result of negligence rather than willful malfeasance? If so, what is the proper sanction?
conclusions: Justice Chambers’ opinion for the Court concluded that substantial evidence supported the hearing officer’s findings regarding Stansfield’s motives and state of mind and that the disciplinary board erred in failing to adopt them. The Court also held that the disciplinary board erred in finding that the vulnerability of the victim constituted an aggravating factor with regard to Stansfield’s violation of §1.2(f) insofar as there was no evidence that Stansfield, having never met his purported client in person, was aware of the characteristics that rendered them vulnerable or in any way acted to exploit them. Thus, the Court reduced Stansfield’s penalty to a reprimand and restitution to his clients.

title: In re detention of Young
facts: Petitioner Andre Young initiated a proceeding pursuant to Washington Revised Code §71.09.090 to show that he no longer met the definition of a sexually violent predator and should be released from commitment. After it was determined that Young had presented sufficient evidence to entitle him to an evidentiary hearing in the Superior Court for King County, the respondent state of Washington requested that Young submit to a psychological examination, which Young refused. The superior court subsequently found Young in contempt of court and ordered him to remain committed until he complied with the state’s request. Young appealed the contempt order to the Washington Court of Appeals, asserting that it violated Washington Court Rules §37(b)(2)(D), which permits courts to treat as a contempt of court the failure to comply with any court order except an order to submit to a physical or mental examination. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the superior court’s order. Young appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: May a court hold an accused sexually violent predator in contempt of court for refusing to submit to a psychological examination?
conclusions: Justice Charles W. Johnson’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that the exception created by §37(b)(2)(D) for refusals to submit to physical or mental examinations conflicts with the civil and criminal contempt provisions of Washington Revised Code §7.21 and that §7.21 controls. Thus, as the superior court had in the Court’s view acted within the authority granted by §7.21 in holding Young in contempt of court and imposing a remedial sanction designed to coerce compliance, the Court remanded the case to the superior court.

title: Brutsche v. Kent
facts: Petitioner Leo Brutsche filed suit against the respondent city of Kent in the Superior Court for King County after police damaged the doors to several buildings on Brutsche’s property while executing a search warrant, asserting that the damage to his property in the course of a search that yielded no evidence constituted trespass and a compensable taking under Article I §16 of the Washington State Constitution and the 5th Amendment to the United States Constitution insofar as the officers acted unreasonably under the circumstances given that he had cooperated with the search and offered to open with his keys the buildings that were ultimately forced open using battering rams. The trial court granted summary judgment for the city of Kent, ruling that the officers had acted reasonably and in accordance with standard procedures. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court’s decision. Brutsche appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the officers searching Brutsche’s property commit trespass by engaging in unreasonable conduct in exercising their privilege to be on Brutsche’s property? Does the damage to Brutsche’s property constitute a compensable taking?
conclusions: Justice Madsen’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, holding that, given the risks to officer safety inherent to searches for the manufacture of methamphetamines, the officers’ conduct of the search was reasonable under the circumstances and did not constitute trespass. The Court also concluded that property damage occurring during the execution of a search warrant does not constitute a taking.

title: Washington v. Montgomery
facts: Petitioner Virgil Montgomery was convicted of possession of pseudoephedrine with intent to manufacture methamphetamine in the Superior Court for Spokane County after police observed him behaving suspiciously and purchasing large quantities of several of the necessary ingredients for manufacturing methamphetamine. Montgomery subsequently appealed his conviction, asserting that the evidence against him was insufficient to convict him, that the testimony of the police officers that arrested him constituted inadmissible opinion testimony, and that the trial court erred in instructing the jury that it could infer from the absence of several potential witnesses on Montgomery’s behalf that their testimony would have been unfavorable.
questions: Was the evidence against Montgomery sufficient to convict him? If so, did the testimony of the police officers that arrested Montgomery constitute inadmissible opinion testimony? If so, was the error harmless? Did the trial court err in instructing the jury that it could infer from the absence of several potential witnesses on Montgomery’s behalf that their testimony would have been unfavorable?
conclusions: Justice Chambers’ opinion for the Court vacated Montgomery’s conviction and remanded the case to the trial court for retrial, concluding that although the evidence against Montgomery was sufficient to convict him given that the jury was not required to believe his legitimate explanations for his suspicious behavior and purchases and although the trial court’s error in admitting opinion testimony regarding Montgomery’s guilt on the part of the officers that arrested Montgomery was harmless, Montgomery is nonetheless entitled to a new trial due to the trial court’s error in instructing the jury that it could infer from the absence of several potential witnesses on Montgomery’s behalf that their testimony would have been unfavorable. In particular, as the testimony of these witnesses would merely have been cumulative and as their absence was adequately explained, the Court held that the missing witness instruction was erroneous and prejudicial to Montgomery.

title: Brundridge v. Fluor Federal Services, Inc.
facts: Respondent Scott Brundridge was fired from his job as a pipefitter with petitioner Fluor Federal Services, Inc. after he and other workers raised safety concerns regarding working conditions. Claiming that he had been wrongfully discharged in violation of public policy, Brundridge subsequently filed suit against Fluor Federal Services in the Superior Court for Benton County. Following a trial, the jury found for Brundridge, who was awarded back pay, front pay, and damages for emotional distress. Asserting that Brundridge had failed to establish the “jeopardy” element of the tort of wrongful discharge, that the trial court had erred in admitting evidence of prior bad acts, and that jury’s award was excessive, Fluor Federal Services appealed the decision and the award. The Washington Court of Appeals certified the case to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the Supreme Court of Washington’s decision in the interim in Korslund v. DynCorp Tri-Cities preclude Brundridge from establishing the “jeopardy” element of the tort of wrongful discharge? Did the trial court err in admitting evidence of prior bad acts on the part of Fluor Federal Services? Was the jury’s award excessive? Is Brundridge entitled to costs?
conclusions: Justice Owens’ opinion for the Court affirmed the trial court’s decision, holding that although the Court’s decision in Korslund represented an intervening change in law with regard to the “jeopardy” element of the tort of wrongful discharge, Fluor Federal Services had waived its right to argue the “jeopardy” element at trial. The Court also concluded that although the trial court had erred in admitting evidence of prior bad acts, the error was harmless. The Court also affirmed the jury's award, finding that the damages awarded to Brundridge were not excessive as they were not unmistakably the product of passion or prejudice. Finally, the Court also ruled that Brundridge was not entitled to costs as no evidence had been presented that misconduct by Fluor Federal Services contributed to excessive costs.

title: Harry v. Buse Timber & Sales, Inc.
facts: Respondent Donald Harry filed a permanent partial disability claim pursuant to Washington Revised Code §51.32.180(b) against his former employer, petitioner Buse Timber & Sales, Inc., after it was revealed that he had suffered permanent hearing loss as a result of workplace exposure to loud noise during his employment at Buse Timber & Sales. The Department of Labor and Industries ordered Buse Timber & Sales to compensate Harry according to the schedule of benefits in place in 1974, the date when an audiogram first revealed that Harry was suffering hearing loss. Harry appealed the order, asserting that he should be compensated according to the schedule of benefits in place in 2001, the date when it was revealed that the hearing loss was partially disabling. After both the Board of Industrial Appeals and the superior court affirmed the Department of Labor and Industries' order, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed, holding that progressive hearing loss should be treated as multiple injuries rather than a single injury, with compensation determined according to the schedule of benefits in place at the time of each incremental loss. Buse Timber & Sales appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Which schedule of benefits governs compensation under §51.32.180(b) for disabilities such as hearing loss that are the cumulative result of working under injurious conditions over an extended period of time?
conclusions: Justice Madsen's opinion for the Court concluded that rather than applying multiple schedules of benefits for multiple incremental hearing losses, §51.32.180(b) requires that Harry be compensated according the schedule of benefits in place at the time of Harry's last exposure to loud noise in the workplace as it was at this date that Harry's injury was complete. Thus, the Court ordered that Harry be compensated according to the schedule of benefits in place at the time of his retirement in 2001.

title: In re disciplinary proceeding against Trejo
facts: Petitioner George Trejo Jr. was charged by the Washington State Bar Association with three counts of misconduct arising out of his trust accounting procedures and lack of oversight of a non-lawyer assistant in violation of former Washington Rules of Professional Conduct §1.14(b)(3), §1.14(a), and §5.3(b). The discipline hearing officer recommended a six-month suspension from practicing the law, but the Disciplinary Board reduced the suspension to three-months along with a two-year probation after applying an additional mitigating factor of character and reputation because of Trejo’s extensive pro bono hours. Trejo appealed the suspension arguing both the hearing officer and the Board misapplied the ABA standards of aggravating and mitigating factors, and thus erred in the findings of facts. The Supreme Court of Washington granted Trejo’s petition for review.
questions: Is the hearing officer’s finding that Trejo told the State Bar auditor that he failed to maintain a personal or business account in Washington to protect his assets from creditors supported by substantial evidence? Is the hearing officer’s finding that Trejo deposited nonrefundable retainers into a client trust account supported by substantial evidence? Is a three-month suspension followed by a two-year probation an appropriate sanction?
conclusions: Justice Fairhurst’s opinion for the Court upheld the hearing officer’s and the Board’s findings that Trejo knowingly violated Washington Rules of Professional Conduct §1.14(b)(3) and §5.3(b) by failing to review the bank statements in question and failing to reconcile them with his office accounts. In addition, he knowingly failed to discover that his assistant was embezzling funds from a commingled client trust account, since he was aware of his obligation to supervise employees and to maintain adequate records regarding client accounts. Further, Trejo knowingly violated Washington Rule of Professional Conduct §1.14(a) by indicating to the State Bar auditor that he deposited all earned funds into his client trust account to keep his fees from the grasp of his creditors. Holding the hearing officer and Board were correct in the findings of fact and weighing the aggravating and mitigating factors, Trejo’s three-month suspension and two-year probation was imposed.

title: Community Telecable of Seattle, Inc. v. Seattle
facts: After paying city utility taxes associated with its provision of high speed cable internet service at the 6% telecommunications services rate rather than at the 0.415% business and occupation tax rate under protest, petitioner Community Telecable of Seattle, Inc. filed suit against the respondent city of Seattle in the Superior Court for King County seeking recovery of the difference on grounds that the definition of “network telephone service” under Washington Revised Code §82.04.065(2) does not include high speed cable internet service. The trial court granted summary judgment for Community Telecable of Seattle. However, the Washington Court of Appeals subsequently reversed the trial court’s decision and granted summary judgment for the city of Seattle. Community Telecable of Seattle appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: May high speed cable internet service be taxed at the telecommunications services rate?
conclusions: Justice Stephens’ opinion for a unanimous Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals and reinstated the trial court’s granting of summary judgment for Community Telecable of Seattle, holding that as data is transformed and manipulated in the provision of high speed cable internet service, such service does not constitute “network telephone service” under §82.04.065(2) and cannot be taxed at the telecommunications services rate.

title: Washington v. Setterstrom
facts: Michael Setterstrom was convicted of possessing a controlled substance in the Superior Court for Thurston County after a frisk of his person and search of his backpack by a police officer that was occasioned by Setterstrom’s erratic behavior while under the influence of methamphetamine revealed methamphetamine and drug paraphernalia. Setterstrom subsequently appealed his conviction, asserting that the frisk of his person that precipitated the search of his backpack was in violation of the 4th Amendment to the United States Constitution and Article II §7 of the Washington State Constitution insofar as it was not based upon a reasonable belief that Setterstrom was armed and presently dangerous. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Setterstrom’s conviction. Setterstrom appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Was the frisk of Setterstrom’s person justified by a reasonable belief that Setterstrom was armed and presently dangerous?
conclusions: Justice James M. Johnson’s opinion for a unanimous Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals and vacated Setterstrom’s conviction, concluding that the frisk was not justified by a reasonable belief that Setterstrom was armed and presently dangerous given that, despite being under the influence of methamphetamine and acting erratically, Setterstrom made no threatening gestures or statements.

title: Tesoro Refining & Marketing Company v. Department of Revenue
facts: Seeking a refund of hazardous substance taxes that it had paid for refinery gas produced at one of its refineries pursuant to Washington Revised Code §82.21, petitioner Tesoro Refining & Marketing Company filed suit against the respondent Department of Revenue in the Superior Court for Thurston County, asserting that the refinery gas is not taxable under §82.21 as it is a byproduct that is not sold or distributed but rather used solely within the refinery for heating purposes. The trial court granted summary judgment for the Department of Revenue. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court’s decision. Tesoro appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Is Tesoro’s possession and use of refinery gas in its refinery taxable under §82.21?
conclusions: Justice Fairhurst’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that §82.21’s definition of the term “control” as the power to sell or use a hazardous substance or to authorize its sale or use by another is disjunctive rather than conjunctive and encompasses Tesoro’s production and internal use of refinery gas. The Court also held that §82.21 renders obsolete any interpretation of Washington Administrative Code §458-20-252(7)(b) as granting a tax exemption for refinery gas.

title: In re marriage of Kowalewski
facts: Petitioner Mariusz Kowalewski petitioned the Superior Court for Pierce County to vacate provisions of a divorce decree that it had previously issued dividing real property located in Poland between Kowalewski and his former wife, asserting that the court lacked jurisdiction to award title to property located outside of the state of Washington. The superior court rejected Kowalewski’s motion, ruling that the divorce decree was valid insofar as it did not purport to directly affect title to property located in Poland but rather simply divided the parties’ rights and interests in the property. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the superior court’s ruling. Kowalewski appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the superior court have jurisdiction to distribute ownership interests in real property located in Poland?
conclusions: Justice Madsen’s opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that while the superior court lacks jurisdiction to directly affect title to real property located outside of the state of Washington, it does possess jurisdiction to indirectly affect title to such property by apportioning interests among individuals over whom it has personal jurisdiction. Thus, the Court held that the divorce decree was valid as it did not purport to operate as a muniment of title but rather simply determined the parties’ respective rights and interests in the property.

title: Washington v. Eisfeldt
facts: Petitioner Jason Eisfeldt was convicted of unlawful manufacture of a controlled substance in the Superior Court for Thurston County after a contractor performing work in Eisfeldt’s home noticed evidence of marijuana cultivation and notified the police, who subsequently searched the premises and, on the basis of what they discovered, obtained a warrant to conduct a broader search that revealed an active marijuana growing operation. Eisfeldt subsequently appealed his conviction, asserting that the search had violated his rights under the 4th Amendment to the United States Constitution and Article I §7 of the Washington State Constitution. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Eisfeldt’s conviction, holding that the initial warrantless search of Eisfeldt’s home that provided probable cause for the subsequent search was constitutional insofar as it did not go beyond the scope of the private search conducted by Eisfeldt’s contractor. Eisfeldt appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Was the initial warrantless search of Eisfeldt’s home constitutional under the private search doctrine?
conclusions: Justice Sanders’ opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals and ordered the evidence derived from the search of Eisfeldt’s home suppressed, concluding that the right against unreasonable searches and seizures conferred by Article I §7 is broader than that conferred by the 4th Amendment and constitutes a blanket prohibition against warrantless searches subject to a few well defined exceptions that do not include the private search doctrine. Thus, the Court concluded that the warrant to search Eisfeldt’s home lacked probable cause.

title: Briggs v. Nova Services, Inc.
facts: Petitioner Ken Briggs and other employees sought damages from respondent corporate employer Nova Services and its executive director for wrongful termination, in violation of public policy, unlawful retaliation-wrongful discharge, negligent infliction of emotional distress, intentional infliction of emotional distress/outrage, and negligent supervision/retention. The employees confronted the board of directors via letters opposing the executive director’s managerial style, but the board supported the executive director, and as a result of the confrontation six employees quit and two were fired for insubordination. The employees argued their actions constituted “concerted activities” statutorily protected under RCW §49.32.020, which prevented Nova from terminating any of the employees. After being denied a motion for continuance based on the employees’ inability to complete discovery, the Superior Court for Spokane County entered a summary judgment in favor of Nova. On the employees’ appeal, Division Three of the Court of Appeals affirmed on all grounds, holding that the employees did not engage in “concerted activities” protected by RCW §49.36.020 because they employees’ concerns did not relate to a term or condition of employment. The Superior Court of Washington Granted the employees’ petition for review.
questions: Does the employee conduct of directly opposing the managerial style of an executive director, resulting in the willing end to the employee-employer relationship constitute “concerted activities” protected under RCW §49.32.020?
conclusions: Justice James M. Johnson’s opinion for the court affirmed the decision of the Court of Appeals, concluding that Nova did not violate a clear public policy when it fired two employees and accepted the resignation of six others because the record showed that the employees were simply complaining about managerial decisions, and not about wages and hours or harassment. Nor were they complaining about terms and conditions of employment or requesting better benefits, more breaks, or easier rules. Therefore, the terminations did not jeopardize the public policy in RCW §49.32.020, nor were the firings caused by protected activities, and the summary judgment in favor of Nova was upheld.

title: Washington v. Modica
facts: Petitioner Desmond Modica was convicted of assault, resisting arrest, and witness tampering in the Superior Court for King County after striking his wife and subsequently attempting to prevent his wife from testifying via phone calls made to his grandmother while he was in jail awaiting trial. Modica appealed his conviction for witness tampering, asserting that the phone calls to his grandmother were private and had been recorded and used as evidence against him in violation of the Washington Privacy Act (Washington Revised Code §9.73.030). The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Modica’s conviction. Modica appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Were the phone calls Modica made to his grandmother from jail private for purposes of §9.73.030?
conclusions: Justice Chambers’ opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that the phone calls were not private for purposes of §9.73.030 insofar as Modica and his grandmother did not have a reasonable expectation of privacy given the fact that Modica was imprisoned, the fact that a sign adjacent to the phones in the King County Jail warns inmates that their phone calls will be recorded, and the fact that an automated message preceding each phone call that is made from the King County Jail being connected warns both the caller and the recipient that the call will be recorded and is subject to monitoring. Thus, as the communications were not privileged, the Court held that their recording and use against Modica as evidence was not prohibited by §9.73.030.

title: Washington v. Fisher
facts: Petitioner Timothy Fisher was convicted of sexually molesting his former stepdaughter in the Superior Court for Benton County after a trial in which the prosecution, in contravention of a pretrial agreement, discussed allegations of previous physical abuse of other children under Fisher’s care during its opening statement and subsequently introduced evidence of the abuse during direct examination of its first witness. Fisher appealed his conviction, claiming that admitting evidence regarding previous acts of abuse on his part for purposes other than accounting for his former stepdaughter’s delay in reporting the alleged sexual abuse violated his right to a fair trial. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Fisher’s conviction, holding that the evidence was properly admitted at the trial court’s discretion. Fisher appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Was the evidence of previous acts of child abuse by Fisher admissible not only for the purpose of accounting for the delay in reporting the alleged crime but also for the purpose of establishing that Fisher had engaged in a consistent pattern of abusive behavior toward children?
conclusions: Justice Fairhurst’s opinion for the Court concluded that Fisher had been denied a fair trial by the prosecution’s violation of the pretrial agreement, ruling that as evidence of a defendant’s prior misconduct is generally not admissible for purposes of demonstrating the defendant’s propensity to commit the charged crime under Washington Rules of Evidence §404(b), the only circumstance under which the evidence of Fisher’s prior abusive behavior could have been introduced would have been to rebut any attempt by Fisher to have the jury draw a negative inference from his former stepdaughter’s delayed reporting. However, as Fisher did not raise the issue at trial, the evidence was inadmissible and the Court therefore vacated Fisher’s conviction.

title: In re custody of A.C.
facts: Respondent David Nagel and his wife Anita Bangert filed a petition in the Superior Court for Spokane County for custody of A.C., for whom they had previously acted as foster parents prior to A.C. being returned to his mother, petitioner Holly Cork. Cork subsequently moved to have the custody petition dismissed on grounds that Washington lacked subject matter jurisdiction under the Uniform Child Custody Jurisdiction and Enforcement Act (codified in Washington Revised Code §26.27) insofar as Nagel and his wife were residents of Montana and the trial court therefore lacked jurisdiction to overturn a Montana court order granting custody of A.C. to Cork. The trial court denied Cork's motion and awarded custody of A.C. to Nagel and his wife. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals affirmed. Cork appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does Washington have jurisdiction over the custody dispute under the Uniform Child Custody Jurisdiction and Enforcement Act?
conclusions: Justice Chambers' opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, holding that Washington lacked jurisdiction as the Uniform Child Custody Jurisdiction and Enforcement Act provides that a state may not modify a child custody determination made by a court of another state unless all of the parties involved no longer reside in the state that made the initial custody determination or that state declines jurisdiction. Thus, as a Montana district court order had terminated the state's temporary protective custody of A.C. and returned A.C. to Cork and as Montana had not expressly declined jurisdiction, the Court dismissed Nagel's petition for lack of jurisdiction.

title: Washington v. Mines
facts: Petitioner John Mines was convicted of rape, kidnapping, and assault in the Superior Court for Spokane County and sentenced to an indeterminate sentence with an exceptional minimal sentence on grounds that the crimes were committed with deliberate cruelty. Mines subsequently appealed his convictions and sentence, asserting that insufficient evidence supported his convictions and that the exceptional minimal sentence was inconsistent with the United States Supreme Court’s decision in Blakely v. Washington, which held that aggravating factors increasing the penalty for a crime must be submitted to the jury and proven beyond a reasonable doubt. After staying proceedings pending the Supreme Court of Washington’s decision in Washington v. Clarke, which held that aggravating factors supporting an exceptional minimal sentence need not be submitted to the jury and proven beyond a reasonable doubt in cases in which the exceptional minimal sentence does not exceed the statutory maximum sentence and in which substantial and compelling reasons exist for imposing an exceptional sentence, the Washington Court of Appeals certified the case to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Were Mines’ convictions supported by sufficient evidence?
conclusions: Justice Charles W. Johnson’s opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed Mines’ convictions, concluding that sufficient evidence in the form of both physical evidence and eyewitness testimony was presented for the jury to infer that Mines had raped and assaulted the victim. The Court also held that sufficient evidence was presented for the jury to infer that Mines had committed kidnapping by abducting the victim with the intent to commit a felony despite the fact that the victim had initially entered Mines’ automobile voluntarily given that one of Mines’ accomplices had testified that Mines had planned to pick up the victim in order to rob her.

title: Washington v. Kier
facts: Petitioner Herbert Kier was convicted of first degree robbery and second degree assault in the Superior Court for King County after he and an accomplice stole an automobile from its owner and a passenger at gunpoint. Kier subsequently appealed his second degree assault conviction, asserting that it merged into his first degree robbery conviction. The Washington Court of Appeals certified the case to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the second degree assault and the first degree robbery constitute two crimes with separate and distinct purposes? If not, do Kier’s first degree robbery and second degree assault convictions merge?
conclusions: Justice Stephens’ opinion for the Court reversed Kier’s second degree assault conviction and remanded the case to the trial court for resentencing, concluding that the second degree assault and the first degree robbery did not constitute two crimes with separate and distinct purposes given that the purpose and effect of both was to effectuate the carjacking. The Court also held that the second degree assault conviction therefore merges into the first degree robbery conviction insofar as the threat to use force necessary to establish second degree assault elevated the robbery to the first degree.

title: Spain v. Employment Security Department
facts: After resigning from her job due to verbal abuse by her supervisor, petitioner Sara Spain applied for unemployment benefits. The respondent Employment Security Department rejected her application on grounds that individuals who leave their jobs voluntarily for reasons other those specified by Washington Revised Code §50.20.050(2)(b)(i)-(x) as non-disqualifying are not eligible for unemployment benefits. Asserting that the non-disqualifying reasons for leaving a job voluntarily specified by §50.20.050(2)(b)(i)-(x) are not an exhaustive list of the reasons that satisfy Washington Revised Code §50.20.050(2)(a)’s requirement that individuals seeking unemployment benefits who left their jobs voluntarily left their jobs for “good cause,” Spain subsequently filed suit against the Employment Security Department. The trial court ruled for Spain. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed. Spain appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Do the non-disqualifying reasons for leaving a job voluntarily specified by §50.20.050(2)(b)(i)-(x) define “good cause” for purposes of §50.20.050(2)(a)?
conclusions: Justice Chambers’ opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that differences in the language used in the two statutory provisions suggest that “good cause” is not limited to §50.20.050(2)(b)(i)-(x)’s non-disqualifying reasons. Thus, the Court remanded the case to the Employment Security Department to determine whether Spain had “good cause” to leave her job voluntarily.

title: Yousoufian v. Office of Ron Sims
facts: Respondent Armen Yousoufian filed suit against the Office of Ron Sims, the King County Executive, in the Superior Court for King County, alleging that the county had acted in bad faith in failing to timely and fully respond to public records requests relating to stadium financing. The trial court found that the county had been untimely and unreasonable in its response to Yousoufian's request but had not acted in bad faith and based the damages it awarded to Yousoufian upon the minimum per day penalty of $5 established by the Public Records Act (Washington Revised Code §42.56). Yousoufian subsequently appealed to the Washington Court of Appeals, which reversed the trial court's decision, holding that the county had acted with gross negligence, and remanded the case to the trial court, which awarded damages of $15 per day to Yousoufian. Yousoufian appealed the award and the Washington Court of Appeals again reversed the trial court. The county appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the trial court abuse its discretion in awarding damages to Yousoufian?
conclusions: Justice Sanders' opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that the trial court's award of damages of $15 per day was clearly not proportionate to the county's extreme malfeasance as the penalty assessed was at the lower end of the range established by §42.56. Thus, the Court remanded the case to the trial court with instructions to assess a penalty, in light of a multifactor analysis considering specific mitigating and aggravating factors, at the higher end of the range established by §42.56.

title: Verizon Northwest, Inc. v. Employment Security Department
facts: Petitioner Verizon Northwest Inc. sought judicial review of the respondent Employment Security Department’s decision that several managerial employees who chose to participate in a voluntary separation program as part of a reduction in force were qualified to receive unemployment compensation. The Commissioner decided the employees were qualified under the employer-initiated layoff exception (Wash. Admin Code 192-150-100) to the rule that employees who voluntarily leave employment without good cause may not collect unemployment benefits; Wash. Rev. Code §50.20.050(1). The Snohomish County Superior Court affirmed the Commissioner’s ruling, and Verizon’s appeal was transferred to the Supreme Court of Washington for direct review.
questions: Did employee’s who participated in Verizon’s Voluntary Separation Program for Managerial Employees qualify for the WAC 192-150-100 “employer-initiated layoff” exception to the RCW §50.20.050(1) “good cause” to quit rule?
conclusions: Justice Owens’ opinion for the Court held that according to the three requirements for the employer-initiated layoff exception of WAC 192-150-100-- the announcement of a reduction of force, the employee’s offer to be included in the layoff, and the employer’s final action-- all must be established for an employee to qualify. However the record failed to establish Verizon took the final action because there was no evidence that Verizon retained the power to reject volunteering employees. Verizon did not reserve the right to reject any of the offerees and in fact accepted every employee who chose to participate, and therefore did not take the final action. Thus, the Commissioner erred in concluding that the employees were entitled to summary judgment, and the Court reversed the Commissioner’s ruling and entered a summary judgment in favor of Verizon.

title: St. Paul Fire & Marine Insurance Company v. Onvia, Inc.
facts: Responsive Management Systems filed suit against Onvia, Inc. after Onvia sent Responsive Management Systems unsolicited advertisements via fax in violation of state and federal law. Although Onvia tendered the claim to its insurer, St. Paul Fire & Marine Insurance Company, St. Paul Fire & Marine Insurance Company determined that it had no duty to defend or indemnify Onvia and Onvia ultimately employed its own counsel and settled the case. After the settlement assigned all of Onvia’s rights against St. Paul Fire & Marine Insurance Company to Responsive Management Systems, St. Paul Fire & Marine Insurance Company sought a declaratory judgment in the United States District Court for the Western District of Washington that it had had no duty to defend or indemnify Onvia. Responsive Management Systems filed a number of counterclaims asserting that St. Paul Fire & Marine Insurance Company had handled Onvia’s tendering of the claim in bad faith in violation of the Washington Administrative Code and Washington’s Consumer Protection Act (Washingon Revised Code §19.86) by failing to timely acknowledge and act upon the notice of claim and by failing to properly and reasonably investigate the claim. The district court certified to the Supreme Court of Washington the question of whether under Washington law an insured has a cause of action against an insurer for procedural bad faith in cases in which the insurer had no contractual duty to defend or indemnify the insured.
questions: Does an insured have a cause of action under Washington law against an insurer for procedural bad faith in cases in which the insurer had no contractual duty to defend or indemnify the insured? If so, must the insured demonstrate actual harm or does a presumption of harm exist?
conclusions: Justice Stephens’ opinion for a unanimous Court concluded that despite the fact that St. Paul Fire & Marine Insurance Company had no contractual duty to defend or indemnify Onvia, it was nonetheless required to handle Onvia’s tendering of the claim in good faith and is therefore potentially liable for procedural bad faith in violation of the Washington Administrative Code and the Consumer Protection Act. However, the Court also held that no presumption of harm exists in such cases and that actual harm must be demonstrated and recovery limited to proven damages.

title: Lane v. Seattle
facts: Following the Supreme Court of Washington’s decision in Okeson v. Seattle declaring that the provision of streetlights and other analogous services are public functions that must be funded by revenues drawn from cities’ general funds, the respondent city of Seattle ordered Seattle Public Utility to cease charging ratepayers for fire hydrants and instead began using general fund revenues to fund the provision of fire hydrants, raising the tax levied on Seattle Public Utility to defray the cost. After Seattle Public Utility responded by raising water rates to recoup revenues lost to the increased taxes, petitioner Arthur Lane and other ratepayers filed suit against Seattle Public Utility and the city of Seattle in the Superior Court for King County, asserting that Seattle Public Utility must reimburse them for payments made for the provision and maintenance of fire hydrants and that the tax increase imposed by the city of Seattle upon Seattle Public Utility is unconstitutional insofar as it contravenes the spirit of the Okeson decision. The trial court ruled that Seattle Public Utility cannot charge ratepayers for the provision and maintenance of fire hydrants and therefore must reimburse ratepayers but that the increased tax imposed upon Seattle Public Utility by the city of Seattle and the resulting rate increases by Seattle Public Utility are constitutional. Lane appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: May Seattle Public Utility charge ratepayers for the provision and maintenance of fire hydrants? Does Lane have standing to challenge the increased tax imposed upon Seattle Public Utility by the city of Seattle? If so, are the increased tax and Seattle Public Utility’s resulting rate increase constitutional?
conclusions: Justice James M. Johnson’s opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed the trial court, concluding that in light of Okeson Seattle Public Utility cannot constitutionally charge ratepayers for the provision and maintenance of fire hydrants, which are a general government responsibility, and therefore must reimburse ratepayers. The Court also held that Lane has standing to challenge the increased tax imposed upon Seattle Public Utility by the city of Seattle given that the tax is passed on to ratepayers like him directly in the form of increased rates. Finally, the Court ruled that the increased tax and resulting rate increase are constitutional despite Okeson as Okeson does not require that the city of Seattle rely upon a broad-based tax to raise revenue for the provision and maintenance of fire hydrants.

title: Pardee v. Jolly
facts: Petitioner Gary Pardee entered into an agreement to purchase real estate from respondent Willis Jolly. The terms of the agreement stipulated that Pardee would make periodic payments during an initial period in which he could occupy and improve the property prior to exercising an option to purchase the property outright. After Pardee failed to notify Jolly in writing of his intent to purchase the property upon tendering the final payment, Jolly refused to sell the property when Pardee later notified him of his intent to exercise the purchase option. Pardee subsequently filed suit against Jolly for specific performance of the contract. The trial court decided that Pardee is entitled to specific performance insofar as he did not breach the terms of the agreement given that his exercise of the purchase option was contemporaneous with his reissuing of the check he wrote to make his final payment after the first check had been dishonored due to Jolly’s failure to timely cash it. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed, holding in light of new evidence that notification and payment had not been contemporaneous. Pardee appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Is the agreement enforceable? If so, is Pardee entitled to specific performance? If not, is Pardee entitled to an equitable grace period?
conclusions: Justice Fairhurst’s opinion for the Court affirmed in part and reversed in part the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that although the agreement violated the statute of frauds insofar as it did not contain an adequate description of the property, it is enforceable under the part performance exception to the statute of frauds. However, the Court also held that Pardee failed to perform under the terms of the agreement when he failed to exercise the purchase option at the time he first tendered the check. Nonetheless, the Court decided that Pardee may be entitled to an equitable grace period given that the agreement was a hybrid of a lease with an option to purchase and an option contract and therefore remanded the case to the trial court.

title: Washington v. Bahl
facts: Petitioner Eric Bahl was convicted of second degree rape and burglary in the Superior Court for Snohomish County and sentenced to a term of imprisonment to be followed by a life term of community custody. Bahl subsequently appealed his sentence, asserting that the conditions attached to his community custody, which prohibit Bahl from possessing or accessing pornographic materials, from frequenting establishments whose primary business pertains to sexually explicit or erotic material, and from possessing sexual stimulus material for his particular deviancy, are unconstitutionally vague in violation of the 14th Amendment to the United States Constitution and Article I §3 of the Washington State Constitution. The Washington Court of Appeals declined to hear Bahl’s vagueness challenge on grounds that the challenge is not ripe for review insofar as Bahl remains imprisoned and has not been accused of violating any of the conditions. Bahl appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Is Bahl’s vagueness challenge to the conditions attached to his community custody ripe for review? If so, are the conditions unconstitutionally vague?
conclusions: Justice Madsen’s opinion for the Court vacated Bahl’s sentence and remanded the case to the trial court for resentencing, concluding that Bahl’s vagueness challenge is sufficiently ripe for review given that the issues raised by Bahl’s challenge are primarily legal and do not require further factual development and that two of the three conditions attached to Bahl’s community custody are unconstitutionally vague. In particular, the Court found that the condition prohibiting Bahl from possessing or accessing pornographic materials is vague insofar as it does not define what types of materials are pornographic and that the condition prohibiting Bahl from possessing sexual stimulus material for his particular deviancy is vague insofar as Bahl has not been diagnosed with any specific deviancy. However, the Court also found that the condition prohibiting Bahl from frequenting establishments whose primary business pertains to sexually explicit or erotic material is not vague insofar as it represents a complete ban prohibiting Bahl from ever visiting such establishments under any circumstances.

title: Transamerican Capital Corporation v. Gervin
facts: A judgment against petitioner George Gervin was entered in a Texas court after Gervin failed to repay loans to respondent Transamerican Capital Corporation. Transamerican Capital Corporation subsequently registered the foreign judgment with the Superior Court for Pierce County as required by Washington Revised Code §6.36.025 and an order was issued requiring the managing partner of the 401 Group, in which Gervin had a limited partnership interest, to pay Gervin’s share of distributions of income to Transamerican Capital Corporation in order to satisfy the judgment. After Transamerican Capital Corporation attempted to have the order enforced by filing a writ of execution ordering the Pierce County Sheriff’s Department to execute on Gervin’s entire limited partnership interest in the 401 Group, Gervin filed a motion in the Superior Court for Pierce County to quash the writ of execution on grounds that the writ of execution purported to sell an interest that could not be executed on and that the judgment against him had expired. The trial court rejected Gervin’s motion. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals certified the case to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Is the judgment against Gervin expired for purposes of §6.36.025 and therefore unenforceable?
conclusions: Justice Sanders’ opinion for a unanimous Court reversed the trial court and quashed the writ of execution, concluding that the judgment against Gervin had expired for purposes of §6.36.025 given that Washington Revised Code §6.17.020(7) establishes that the lifetime of a registered foreign judgment cannot extend beyond the lifetime of the underlying judgment, which under Texas law had become dormant and expired.

title: Simonetta v. Viad Corporation
facts: After developing lung cancer as a result of exposure to asbestos during his service in the navy performing maintenance on evaporators manufactured by petitioner Viad Corporation that were insulated with asbestos, respondent Joseph Simonetta filed suit against Viad Corporation. The trial court granted summary judgment for Viad Corporation, ruling that Viad Corporation had no duty to warn of the risks of exposure to asbestos given that the asbestos insulation that caused Simonetta’s cancer was applied to the evaporators by the navy subsequent to their manufacture. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed, holding that as the evaporators were designed to utilize asbestos insulation and as there was a danger of asbestos being released in the normal course of their maintenance, Viad Corporation had a duty to warn users and could be held liable for the consequences of exposure to asbestos. Viad Corporation appealed this decision to the Supreme Court.
questions: May Viad Corporation be held liable for the consequences of exposure to asbestos resulting from the use of asbestos insulation in its evaporators despite the fact that it was not involved in manufacturing or distributing the insulation?
conclusions: Justice Charles W. Johnson’s opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals and reinstated the trial court’s granting of summary judgment for Viad Corporation, concluding that the duty to warn is limited to those in the chain of distribution of a hazardous product. Thus, as Viad Corporation was not involved in manufacturing or distributing asbestos insulation, it could not be held liable.

title: Braaten v. Saberhagen Holdings
facts: After developing mesothelioma as a result of exposure to asbestos while working as a pipefitter aboard navy ships, respondent Vernon Braaten filed suit against petitioner Saberhagen Holdings, which manufactured the valves and pumps used aboard the ships Braaten had worked on, in the Superior Court for King County. The trial court dismisseed Braaten’s strict product liability and negligence claims, ruling that as the asbestos insulation that caused Braaten’s mesothelioma was applied to the valves and pumps by the navy subsequent to their manufacture, Saberhagen Holdings had no duty to warn of the risks of exposure to asbestos. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed, holding that as the valves and pumps were designed to utilize asbestos insulation and as there was a danger of asbestos being released in the course of their normal use, Saberhagen Holdings had a duty to warn users. Saberhagen Holdings appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did Saberhagen Holdings have a duty to warn users of its products of the dangers of exposure to asbestos insulation despite the fact that it was not involved in manufacturing or distributing the insulation?
conclusions: Justice Madsen’s opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals and reinstated the trial court’s order of summary judgment for Saberhagen Holdings, concluding that regardless of foreseeability a manufacturer has no duty to warn of the dangers of products it did not manufacture and for which it was not involved in the chain of distribution.

title: McKee v. AT&T Corporation
facts: Respondent Michael McKee filed a class action suit against petitioner AT&T Corporation in the Superior Court for Chelan County, asserting that AT&T wrongfully added city utility surcharges to long distance telephone service bills and charged usurious late fees in violation of Washington’s Consumer Protection Act (Washington Revised Code §19.86) and its usury statute (Washington Revised Code §19.52). AT&T subsequently moved to compel arbitration pursuant to its consumer services agreement, which requires binding arbitration of all disputes. However, the trial court rejected the motion, ruling that the consumer services agreement’s dispute resolution clause is substantively unconscionable insofar as it prohibits class actions, shortens the applicable statute of limitations, limits damages, requires confidentiality, and requires the application of New York law. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals certified the case to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Is the conscionability of the dispute resolution clause determined by New York law or by Washington law? If Washington law governs, is Washington law preempted by either the Federal Communications Act (47 U.S.C. §§151-161, 201-231, 251-261, 301-339, 351-363) or the Federal Arbitration Act (9 U.S.C. §1-14)? If not, is the dispute resolution clause substantively unconscionable?
conclusions: Justice Chambers’ opinion for the Court affirmed the trial court, concluding that the conscionability of the dispute resolution clause is determined by Washington law rather than by New York law despite the clause’s stipulation that New York governs given that Washington law would otherwise apply, that the relevant provisions of New York law conflict with fundamental public policy in the state of Washington insofar as they permit waivers of the right to bring a class action claim, and that Washington’s interest in protecting its consumers outweighs New York’s interest in the matter. The Court also held that Washington law is not preempted by either the Federal Communications Act, which was not intended to preempt state or private remedies, or the Federal Arbitration Act, which does not require the enforcement of unconscionable contract provisions. Finally, the Court ruled that the dispute resolution clause is substantively unconscionable under Washington law as Washington case law has held that contractual provisions of the sort included in the dispute resolution clause that prohibit class actions, shorten applicable statutes of limitation, limit damages, or deny attorney’s fees are substantively unconscionable. Thus, the Court remanded the case for trial.

title: Washington State Major League Baseball Stadium Public Facilities District v. Huber, Hunt & Nichols-Kiewit Construction Company
facts: The petitioner Washington State Major League Baseball Stadium Public Facilities District, the municipal corporation responsible for the ownership and operation of Safeco Field, filed suit against respondent Huber, Hunt & Nichols-Kiewit Construction Company in the Superior Court for King County seeking reimbursement for costs incurred repairing defective work performed by Huber, Hunt & Nichols-Kiewit Construction Company in the construction of Safeco Field. The trial court granted summary judgment to Huber, Hunt & Nichols-Kiewit Construction Company, ruling that the statute of limitations had expired. The Washington State Major League Baseball Stadium Public Facilities District appealed, asserting that its claim was not time barred insofar as it was for the benefit of the state and therefore exempted by Washington Revised Code §4.16.160 from the statute of limitations. The Washington Court of Appeals transferred the appeal to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does the exemption from the statute of limitations for sovereign actions brought for the benefit of the state created by §4.16.160 apply to the Washington State Major League Baseball Stadium Public Facilities District's suit against Huber, Hunt & Nichols-Kiewit Construction Company?
conclusions: Justice Stephens' opinion for the Court held that the construction and maintenance of Safeco Field for public recreation was a sovereign rather than a proprietary function as it had been performed for the common good rather than for the specific benefit or profit of the municipal corporation. Thus, the Court concluded that the Washington State Major League Baseball Stadium Public Facilities District's suit was not time barred and remanded the case to the trial court.

title: Washington v. Gatewood
facts: Petitioner Gary Gatewood was convicted of unlawful possession of a firearm, possession of cocaine, and possession of marijuana in the Superior Court for King County after a search of his person prompted by his nervous reaction to the approach of police officers and subsequent attempt to leave the scene revealed an illegal firearm, cocaine, and marijuana. Gatewood appealed his convictions, asserting that the warrantless search was in violation of the 4th Amendment to the United States Constitution and Article I §7 of the Washington State Constitution. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Gatewood’s convictions, holding that the search was a constitutional investigative stop. Gatewood appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Was the search of Gatewood a constitutional investigative stop?
conclusions: Justice James M. Johnson’s opinion for a unanimous Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that while a warrantless search is permissible pursuant to a constitutional investigative stop, such stops require a reasonable suspicion based upon specific and objective facts that the person stopped has committed or is about to commit a crime and this was not the case with regard to the search of Gatewood as startled or nervous reactions to police officers do not by themselves establish reasonable suspicion. Thus, the Court vacated Gatewood’s conviction and ordered the evidence derived from the search suppressed.

title: Adams v. King County
facts: Following the death of petitioner Nancy Adams’ son Jesse Smith, the King County Medical Examiner allowed a private medical research institute to take Smith’s brain for medical research without Adams’ consent on the basis of Smith's having signed an organ donor card. After learning of the transfer, Adams filed suit against King County in the Superior Court for King County, asserting that the medical examiner had violated the Uniform Anatomical Gift Act (Washington Revised Code §68.50.520-560) as well as committed tortious interference with a dead body, invasion of privacy, conspiracy, and fraud. The trial court granted summary judgment for King County, ruling that §68.50.570 authorized the medical examiner to accept the donation of Smith’s organs and transfer them to a qualifying donee without Adams’ consent given that anatomical gifts become irrevocable upon the death of the donor. Adams appealed and the case was subsequently transferred to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does §68.50.570 authorize the transfer of a donor’s organs to any qualifying donee? If not, was the unauthorized transfer potentially tortious?
conclusions: Justice Owens’ opinion for a unanimous Court reversed the trial court and remanded the case for trial, concluding that although the medical research institute that received Smith’s brain is a qualifying donee under §68.50.570, it was not authorized by §68.50.570 to receive Smith’s brain in this case as Smith had not designated a specific recipient for his gift and hospitals are the only entities permitted by §68.50.570 to receive undesignated gifts. The Court also held that Adams had raised actionable claims of tortious interference with a dead body and conspiracy but had failed to raise an actionable claim of invasion of privacy given that no publication of private autopsy records had occurred and had failed to raise an actionable claim of fraud given that Adams had given consent for a sample of Smith’s brain (but not the entire brain) to be taken for medical research.

title: Washington v. Grande
facts: Petitioner Jeremy Grande was charged with possession of marijuana and possession of drug paraphernalia after a search of his person occasioned by a police officer detecting the odor of marijuana emanating from the automobile that Grande was a passenger in during a traffic stop revealed a pipe containing marijuana. Grande subsequently moved to suppress the evidence derived from the warrantless search of his person on grounds that the search lacked probable cause and was in violation of the 4th Amendment to the United States Constitution and Article I §7 of the Washington State Constitution. The district court granted the motion and ordered the evidence suppressed, ruling that the odor of marijuana emanating from the automobile did not establish sufficient probable cause specific to Grande to justify the search. Upon appeal, the Superior Court for Skagit County reversed. Grande appealed this decision to the Washington Court of Appeals, which certified the case to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the odor of marijuana emanating from the automobile establish sufficient individualized probable cause to search Grande?
conclusions: Justice Charles W. Johnson’s opinion for a unanimous Court reversed the superior court, concluding that as a search of a person must be supported by probable cause specific to that person, the search of Grande lacked probable cause insofar as the odor of marijuana emanating from the automobile could not be clearly associated with Grande given the presence of another person in the automobile. Thus, the Court reinstated the district court's suppression order.

title: Washington v. Unga
facts: Petitioner Leaa Unga was convicted in juvenile court of second degree vehicle prowl and second degree taking of a motor vehicle without permission after confessing to police that he had written graffiti on the interior of a stolen automobile. Unga subsequently appealed his conviction, asserting that his confession had been involuntary and should have been suppressed insofar as it had been elicited by a false promise of immunity on the part of the police officer that interrogated him. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Unga’s convictions, holding that the confession had been voluntary. Unga appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington. In the interim, the state of Washington moved to dismiss the second degree vehicle prowl charge, conceding that the police officer that had interrogated Unga, while not promising full immunity, had promised Unga that he would not be charged for writing the graffiti.
questions: Was Unga’s confession involuntary in light of the false promise of immunity that was made to Unga?
conclusions: Justice Madsen’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding in light of the totality of the circumstances that Unga’s confession had been voluntary despite the false promise of immunity that was made given that Unga had waived his Miranda rights and that there was no evidence that the confession had been coerced. Thus, the Court granted the state’s motion to dismiss the second degree vehicle prowl charge and affirmed Unga’s conviction for second degree taking of a motor vehicle without permission.

title: Washington v. Rafay
facts: Petitioner Glen Burns and Atif Rafay were convicted of murder in the Superior Court for King County. Burns subsequently appealed his conviction but moved to have his attorney withdraw and represent himself pro se after his attorney had filed their opening brief. The Washington Court of Appeals rejected Burns’ motion without setting forth its reasoning. Burns appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington, asserting that Article I §22 of the Washington State Constitution confers a right to self-representation.
questions: Does Article I §22 afford a right of self-representation on appeal?
conclusions: Justice Stephens’ opinion for a unanimous Court concluded that although the 6th Amendment to the United States Constitution does not grants appellants a right to self-representation, the analogous right created by Article I §22, in light of the criteria established by the Court in Washington v. Gunwall, is broader and does grant such a privilege. However, as this right is not absolute and may be overriden by an appellate court’s determination that good cause exists to reject an appellant’s motion to represent themselves pro se, the Court remanded the case to the Washington Court of Appeals for proper consideration of the merits of Burns’ motion.

title: Washington v. Daniels
facts: After her newborn son died in her care, respondent Carissa Daniels was convicted of second degree murder (predicated upon a charge of second degree assault) in the Superior Court for Pierce County. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed Daniels' conviction on grounds that assault could not be a predicate offense for second degree murder and ruled that the state was barred by the prohibition against double jeopardy from retrying Daniels for homicide by abuse as the fact that the jury had opted to convict Daniels of second degree murder rather than homicide by abuse acted as an implied acquittal with regard to the charge of homicide by abuse. The state appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington, which reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, holding that retrying Daniels for homicide by abuse would not subject her to double jeopardy insofar as the jury's silence with regard to the charge of homicide by abuse was not an implied acquittal (as such silence may reflect a divided jury rather than an implied acquittal) and there had been no final conviction terminating Daniels' jeopardy. Daniels subsequently petitioned the Supreme Court for Washington for reconsideration in light of the United States Court of Appeal for the Ninth Circuit's decision in Brazzel v. Washington.
questions: Does the United States Court of Appeal for the Ninth Circuit's decision in Brazzel v. Washington compel a different result with regard to the question of whether retrying Daniels for homicide by abuse would subject her to double jeopardy?
conclusions: Justice Charles W. Johnson's opinion for the Court reaffirmed the Court's earlier opinion, concluding that nothing in the United States Court of Appeal for the Ninth Circuit's decision in Brazzel v. Washington compelled a different result.

title: Mutual of Enumclaw Insurance Company v. U.S.F. Insurance Company
facts: Alleging defective construction, the Windsong Arbor Homeowners’ Association filed suit against Dally Homes, Inc., which had constructed the Windsong Arbor condominiums, in the Superior Court for King County. After Dally Homes, which was insured by both the respondent Mutual of Enumclaw Insurance Company and the petitioner U.S.F. Insurance Company, tendered the claim to Mutual of Enumclaw Insurance Company but not to U.S.F. Insurance Company, a settlement was reached. Mutual of Enumclaw Insurance Company subsequently filed suit against U.S.F. Insurance Company in the Superior Court for King County seeking partial reimbursement. The trial court granted summary judgment for U.S.F. Insurance Company, ruling that as Dally Homes had not tendered the claim to U.S.F. Insurance Company, U.S.F. Insurance Company was excused from its duty to perform under the policy or contribute to the settlement under the “selective tender” rule. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the “selective tender” rule is incompatible with and superseded by the “late tender” rule, which stipulates that an insurer must perform under the policy even in instances in which the insured has breached provisions of the policy requiring timely notice unless the insurer is able to demonstrate that the late notice caused it actual and substantial prejudice. U.S.F. Insurance Company appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does the “selective tender” or the “late tender” rule apply to Dally Homes’ claim?
conclusions: Justice Owens’ opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals on alternate grounds, concluding that while Mutual of Enumclaw Insurance Company has no right to equitable contribution given that both insurers were contractually obligated to cover the entire loss, Mutual of Enumclaw Insurance Company may bring a subrogation claim against U.S.F. Insurance Company given that Dally Homes assigned its rights against additional insurers to Mutual of Enumclaw Insurance Company as part of the settlement agreement and the “late tender” rule allows an insured to tender a claim at any time absent actual and substantial prejudice to the insurer. Thus, as U.S.F. Insurance Company had not demonstrated as a matter of law that it was actually and substantially prejudiced by its lack of notice insofar as it had not demonstrated that the lack of notice deprived it of the ability to put forth defenses or to contest the amount of damages, the Court remanded the case to the trial court.

title: In re disciplinary proceeding against Sanai
facts: Petitioner Cyrus Sanai was disbarred after a hearing held by the respondent Washington State Bar Association’s disciplinary committee following allegations of frivolous litigation, disobedience of court orders, and conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice. Sanai subsequently appealed the committee’s decision to the Supreme Court of Washington, asserting that the hearing officer had acted improperly and denied him the opportunity to be heard in refusing his request to delay the hearing for medical reasons, which resulted in the hearing being held in Sanai’s absence.
questions: Did the hearing officer abuse their discretion in refusing Sanai’s request to delay the hearing?
conclusions: Justice Madsen’s opinion for the Court concluded that the hearing officer had, in light of the need for prompt disposition of the case, the needs of and possible prejudice to the parties involved, the prior history of the case, and other material factors abused their discretion in rejecting Sanai’s request as Sanai had provided a doctor’s note and extensive medical testimony that detailed the reasons for his inability to appear. Thus, the Court vacated the disciplinary committee’s decision and remanded the case. [Original Docket Number: 200,560-8]

title: Thurston County v. Western Washington Growth Management Hearings Board
facts: Pursuant to the requirements of the Growth Management Act (Washington Revised Code §36.70A), petitioner Thurston County updated its comprehensive plan and reviewed (but ultimately retained) its urban growth area designations. The respondent Western Washington Growth Management Hearings Board subsequently rejected the comprehensive plan and its urban growth area designations, ruling that it created urban growth areas that significantly exceeded the projected demand for urban residential lands and failed to provide for a variety of rural densitites. Thurston County sought direct review of the board’s decision in the Supreme Court of Washington, which transferred the case to the Washington Court of Appeals. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the board’s decision. Thurston County appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does a growth management hearings board have jurisdiction to review all aspects of a comprehensive plan when a comprehensive plan is updated and its urban growth area designations reviewed pursuant to the Growth Management Act? Does an urban growth area violate the Growth Management Act when the amount of developable residential land in the urban growth area exceeds the projected demand for such land by 38%? Does a comprehensive plan provide for a variety of rural densitites in accordance with the Growth Management Act when resource lands and densities greater than one dwelling unit per five acres are included in the rural component?
conclusions: Justice Fairhurst’s opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed in part and reversed in part the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that a growth management hearings board has jurisdiction to review only those aspects of a comprehensive plan that are directly affected by new or recently amended Growth Management Act provisions following periodic updates to a plan and that a failure to revise urban growth area designations may only be reviewed if the population projection for the county has changed. Thus, the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals’ holding that the Western Washington Growth Management Hearings Board had jurisdiction to review whether Thurston County’s urban growth areas violate the Growth Management Act and whether Thurston County’s comprehensive plan provides for a variety of rural densities. However, the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals’ holding that a county must identify and justify the use of a land market supply factor in making its urban growth area designations and its holding that densities greater than one dwelling unit per five acres cannot be included in the rural component of a comprehensive plan and remanded the case to the Western Washington Growth Management Hearings Board to consider whether Thurston County’s urban growth area designations were clearly erroneous in light of local circumstances and whether the various densities included by Thurston County in the rural component of its comprehensive plan and its use of innovative zoning techniques provide for a variety of rural densitites.

title: Rental Housing Association of Puget Sound v. Des Moines
facts: The petitioner Rental Housing Association of Puget Sound filed suit against the respondent city of Des Moines in the Superior Court for King County, claiming that the city's response to its public records request had failed to comply with Washington Revised Code §42.56. The trial court subsequently granted the city's motion for summary judgment, ruling that the suit was time barred as the Rental Housing Association of Puget Sound had failed to bring its suit within one year of a claim of exception or production of record as required by §42.56.550(6). The Rental Housing Association of Puget Sound appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: When did the statute of limitations imposed by §42.56.550(6) begin to toll?
conclusions: Justice Stephens' opinion for the Court reversed the trial court's granting of summary judgment to the city, holding that the one year statute of limitations did not begin to toll after the city's initial reply to the Rental Housing Association of Puget Sound's request as this reply did not adequately describe withheld records by specifiying which exemptions their withholding was predicated upon. Thus, the city did not state a proper claim of exemption triggering the statute of limitations until it provided the Rental Housing Association of Puget Sound with a detailed privilege log providing this information. As the Rental Housing Association of Puget Sound had filed suit within one year of being provided with the privilege log, its suit was timely and the Court therefore remanded the case to the trial court.

title: Tukwila v. Garrett
facts: Respondent Kellas Garrett was convicted of violating a temporary protection order in the Tukwila Municipal Court and sentenced.
